claim: A genome-wide association study on 15,453 UL cases and 392,628 controls was performed.
source: A genome-wide association study on 15,453 UL cases and 392,628 controls was performed, followed by replication of the genomic risk in six cohorts.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample sizes used in the GWAS.

claim: 22 loci displayed a genome-wide significant association with uterine leiomyoma.
source: 22 loci displayed a genome-wide significant association.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of genome-wide significant loci identified in the study.

claim: TERT, TERC, OBFC1, TP53, and ATM are genes involved in genome stability that are associated with UL predisposition.
source: Genes involved in genome stability were represented by TERT, TERC, OBFC1 - highlighting the role of telomere maintenance - TP53 and ATM.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists these genes as being involved in genome stability and associated with UL predisposition.

claim: WNT4, WT1, SALL1, MED12, ESR1, GREB1, FOXO1, DMRT1, and CD44 are genes involved in genitourinary development that are associated with UL predisposition.
source: Genes involved in genitourinary development, WNT4, WT1, SALL1, MED12, ESR1, GREB1, FOXO1, DMRT1 and uterine stem cell marker antigen CD44, formed another strong subgroup.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists these genes as being involved in genitourinary development and associated with UL predisposition.

claim: The combined risk contributed by the 22 loci was associated with MED12 mutation-positive tumors.
source: The combined risk contributed by the 22 loci was associated with MED12 mutation-positive tumors.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this association between the genomic risk score and MED12 mutation status.

claim: The findings in part explain the more frequent occurrence of UL in women of African origin.
source: The findings link genes for uterine development and genetic stability to leiomyomagenesis, and in part explain the more frequent occurrence of UL in women of African origin.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the findings help explain the increased prevalence in African ancestry populations.

claim: Approximately 70% of women develop ULs before menopause.
source: They are extremely common; approximately 70% of women develop ULs before menopause (Stewart et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support this prevalence estimate.

claim: UL symptoms occur in one fifth of women.
source: The symptoms, occurring in one fifth of women, include excessive menstrual bleeding, abdominal pain and pregnancy complications (Stewart et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support this symptom prevalence.

claim: The annual cost of treating ULs has been approximated to be as high as $34 billion in the United States.
source: ULs cause a substantial human and economic burden, and the annual cost of treating these tumors has been approximated to be as high as $34 billion in the United States, higher than the combined cost of treating breast and colon cancer (Cardozo et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support this cost estimate.

claim: Earlier studies have indicated strong genetic influence in UL susceptibility based on linkage, population disparity, and twin studies.
source: Earlier studies have indicated strong genetic influence in UL susceptibility based on linkage (Gross, 2000), population disparity (Wise et al., 2012) and twin studies (Luoto et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple published studies to support the genetic influence on UL susceptibility.

claim: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) syndrome is caused by high-penetrance germline mutations in the Fumarate hydratase (FH) gene.
source: The most striking UL predisposing condition thus far characterized is hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) syndrome, caused by high-penetrance germline mutations in the Fumarate hydratase (FH) gene (Multiple Leiomyoma Consortium et al., 2002; Launonen et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support this genetic cause of HLRCC syndrome.

claim: Most ULs show somatic site-specific mutations at exons 1 and 2 of the mediator complex subunit 12 (MED12) gene.
source: Most ULs show somatic site-specific mutations at exons 1 and 2 of the mediator complex subunit 12 (MED12) gene (Mäkinen et al., 2011; Heinonen et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support this observation about MED12 mutations.

claim: At least three mutually exclusive UL subtypes have been identified: MED12 mutant, FH deficient, and HMGA2 overexpressing lesions.
source: These observations together with further scrutiny of driver mutations, chromosomal aberrations, gene expression, and clinicopathological characteristics have led to identification of at least three mutually exclusive UL subtypes; MED12 mutant, Fumarate Hydratase (FH) deficient, as well as High Mobility Group AT-Hook 2 (HMGA2) overexpressing lesions (Mehine et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the identification of these UL subtypes.

claim: At discovery stage 1,428 SNPs emerging from 22 distinct genetic loci passed the genome-wide significance level of 5 × 10−8.
source: At discovery stage 1,428 SNPs emerging from 22 distinct genetic loci passed the genome-wide significance level of 5 × 10−8.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of SNPs and loci that reached genome-wide significance.

claim: Two of the significant loci (359/1,428 SNPs) were found on the X chromosome.
source: Two of the significant loci (359/1,428 SNPs) were found on the X chromosome.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of X chromosome loci and SNPs.

claim: After linkage disequilibrium pruning, a total of 50 LD-independent associations remained from the discovery stage.
source: After linkage disequilibrium (LD; r2 ≤0.3) pruning the significant SNPs, a total of 50 LD-independent associations remained: the resulting SNPs are given in Appendix 1—table 2, and the lead SNPs are summarized in Table 1.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of LD-independent associations after pruning.

claim: The initial GRS of 50 SNPs was significantly associated with the UL phenotype in the Helsinki cohort (p=8.3 × 10−10).
source: We applied this initial GRS of 50 SNPs to the Helsinki cohort and identified a significant association to the UL phenotype (p=8.3 × 10−10; adjusted p=1.1 × 10−8; one-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum; W = 1.69 × 106; 457 cases and 8899 female controls).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between the GRS and UL phenotype in the Helsinki cohort.

claim: rs117245733 at 13q14.11 showed suggestive association in both UKBB (OR = 1.26; p=4.2 × 10−9) and Helsinki (OR = 1.82; p=8.1 × 10−6) cohorts.
source: The genome-wide statistics revealed rs117245733, at 13q14.11, as the only SNP with a suggestive (p<10−5) association in both the UKBB (OR = 1.26; p=4.2 × 10−9) and Helsinki (OR = 1.82; p=8.1 × 10−6) cohorts.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the association statistics for this SNP in both cohorts.

claim: The meta-analysis identified altogether 112 genome-wide significant SNPs not seen in the discovery stage.
source: The meta-analysis identified altogether 112 genome-wide significant SNPs not seen in the discovery stage: seven of those were LD-independent (r2 ≤0.3; Appendix 1-table 3) and their UKBB log-odds weights were appended to the initial GRS model.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of additional genome-wide significant SNPs identified in the meta-analysis.

claim: The final GRS model consisted of 57 SNPs.
source: The final GRS model of 57 SNPs and their UKBB-based weights is given in Appendix 1—table 4.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of SNPs in the final GRS model.

source: In NFBC, the SNP identified in the stage two meta-analysis, rs117245733 at 13q14.11, was replicated (p=0.034; linear mixed model; OR = 1.50; 95% CI 1.03 – 2.19).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the replication statistics for this SNP in NFBC.

claim: The association between the GRS and UL phenotype was significant in NFBC (p=1.1 ×10−5).
source: The association between the GRS and UL phenotype was significant (p=1.1 ×10−5; Wilcoxon rank-sum; adjusted p=1.1 × 10−4; one-tailed; W = 4.7 × 105) in NFBC.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between GRS and UL phenotype in NFBC.

claim: The GRS model replicated with a significant phenotype association in all five ethnicities tested.
source: The GRS model replicated with a significant phenotype association in all five ethnicities (Appendix 1-Table 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the GRS replicated across all five ethnic groups tested.

claim: Self-reported 'Black African' individuals had a mean GRS of 4.83 compared to 4.04 for 'White Irish' individuals.
source: The self-reported 'Black African' (mean GRS 4.83) had an outstanding risk-load compared to Caucasian (self-reported 'White Irish'; mean GRS 4.04) background (Figure 4; Wilcoxon rank-sum p<10−15).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the mean GRS values for these two ethnic groups.

claim: The African ethnicity displayed an increased UL prevalence (19%) compared to the Irish (6%).
source: As expected (Wise et al., 2012), the African ethnicity displayed an increased prevalence (19%) compared to the Irish (6%).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the prevalence rates for these two ethnic groups and cites a previous study.

claim: The GRS difference between African and Irish ancestries explains 9.0% of the increased prevalence in the African population.
source: Assuming that the observed GRS weights have a linear relationship to the true risk, the GRS difference between African and Irish ancestries explains 9.0% of the increased prevalence in the African population.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this calculated contribution of GRS to prevalence difference.

claim: Based on gnomAD frequencies, the increased GRS of African ancestry explains between 8 – 16% of the population difference in UL prevalence.
source: Based on the gnomAD frequencies, the increased GRS of African ancestry explains between 8 – 16% of this population difference.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this calculated range for the contribution of GRS to prevalence difference.

claim: The number of ULs per patient had a significant positive association to GRS (p=0.001; rate ratio 1.25).
source: The number of ULs per patient had a significant positive association to GRS (negative binomial regression p=0.001; adjusted p=0.0032; rate ratio 1.25; 95% CI 1.09 – 1.43 for one-unit increase in GRS; Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between number of ULs and GRS.

claim: No association was found between GRS and age at hysterectomy.
source: No association was found between GRS and age at hysterectomy (Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of association between these variables.

claim: The UL set included 1159 (78%) mutation-positive and 322 mutation-negative tumors.
source: Our UL set of 1481 lesions included 1159 (78%) mutation-positive and 322 mutation-negative tumors.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the numbers and percentages of mutation-positive and mutation-negative tumors.

claim: 221 (48%) patients had all their tumors identified as MED12-mutation-positive.
source: In total 221 (48%) and 123 (27%) patients had all their tumors identified as either MED12-mutation-positive or -negative, respectively, suggesting that genetic or environmental factors contribute to the preferred UL type in affected individuals, as previously observed (Mäkinen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number and percentage of patients with all MED12-mutation-positive tumors.

claim: 123 (27%) patients had all their tumors identified as MED12-mutation-negative.
source: In total 221 (48%) and 123 (27%) patients had all their tumors identified as either MED12-mutation-positive or -negative, respectively, suggesting that genetic or environmental factors contribute to the preferred UL type in affected individuals, as previously observed (Mäkinen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number and percentage of patients with all MED12-mutation-negative tumors.

claim: The 221 mutation positive patients had a significantly higher GRS (p=7.9 × 10−4).
source: Indeed, the 221 mutation positive patients were found to have a significantly higher GRS (Wilcoxon rank-sum p=7.9 × 10−4; adjusted p=0.0032; two-sided; W = 1.6 × 104).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between MED12 mutation status and GRS.

claim: The MED12-mutation-positive subset of patients had an odds ratio of 2.28 for one-unit increase in GRS compared to controls.
source: Comparison against the population controls (n = 8899 females) revealed that the above-mentioned patient groups differ by their effect size: the MED12-mutation-positive (221) subset of patients had an odds ratio of 2.28 for one-unit increase in GRS (95% CI 1.80 – 2.88) compared to the controls, while the mutation-negative (123) subset had an odds ratio of 1.20 (95% CI 0.88 – 1.66).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the odds ratio for the MED12-mutation-positive patient subset.

claim: The mutation-negative subset of patients had an odds ratio of 1.20 for one-unit increase in GRS compared to controls.
source: Comparison against the population controls (n = 8899 females) revealed that the above-mentioned patient groups differ by their effect size: the MED12-mutation-positive (221) subset of patients had an odds ratio of 2.28 for one-unit increase in GRS (95% CI 1.80 – 2.88) compared to the controls, while the mutation-negative (123) subset had an odds ratio of 1.20 (95% CI 0.88 – 1.66).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the odds ratio for the mutation-negative patient subset.

claim: The number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors per patient had a significant positive association to GRS (p=3.2 × 10−4; rate ratio 1.43).
source: The number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors per patient had a significant positive association to GRS (p=3.2 × 10−4; adjusted p=0.002; negative binomial model rate ratio 1.43; 95% CI 1.13 – 3.83 for one-unit increase in GRS; Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors and GRS.

claim: No association between the number of MED12-mutation-negative tumors and GRS was found.
source: No association between the number of MED12-mutation-negative tumors and GRS was found (adjusted p=0.053; Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of association between number of MED12-mutation-negative tumors and GRS.

claim: The risk allele rs5937008 near MED12 significantly increased the number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors (p=0.0087; rate ratio 1.23).
source: Strikingly, the risk allele (rs5937008) did significantly increase the number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors (p=0.0087; negative binomial model rate ratio 1.23; 95% CI 1.05 – 1.44).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between this risk allele and number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors.

claim: Among the 457 patients, the median number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors increased from one to two for the risk allele carriers.
source: Among our 457 patients, the median number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors increased from one to two for the risk allele carriers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the change in median number of tumors associated with the risk allele.

claim: In total 34 and 24 genes passed the local permutation significance threshold (p<0.05) for tumor and matched myometrium data, respectively, in eQTL analysis.
source: In total 34 and 24 genes passed the local permutation significance threshold (p<0.05) for tumor and matched myometrium data, respectively (Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of genes passing the significance threshold in eQTL analysis.

claim: Among the eQTL hits in tumors were WNT4 (p=0.01), CDC42 (p=0.03), TNRC6B (p=0.02), FOXO1 (p=0.03), and DMRT1 (p=0.04).
source: Among the hits in tumors were WNT4 (p=0.01; permutation test) and CDC42 (p=0.03) at 1 p, TNRC6B (p=0.02) at 22q, FOXO1 (p=0.03) at 13q, and DMRT1 (p=0.04) at 9 p.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the eQTL associations for these genes in tumors.

claim: None of the local eQTL associations passed a genome-wide FDR of 10%.
source: None of the local associations passed a genome-wide FDR of 10%.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no eQTL associations reached genome-wide significance.

claim: No significant association was observed between the risk allele and MED12 expression.
source: No significant association was observed between the risk allele and MED12 expression (rs5936989; Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of association between the risk allele and MED12 expression.

claim: Analysis of the 57 GRS SNPs revealed altogether 17,030 cis-meQTLs with nominal p<0.05.
source: Our analysis of the 57 GRS SNPs revealed altogether 17,030 (9,466 in tumors and 7564 in matched myometrium) cis methylation quantitative trait loci (cis-meQTL) with nominal p<0.05.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of cis-meQTLs identified.

claim: 145 cis-meQTLs passed a 10% FDR.
source: Of these, 145 passed a 10% FDR.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of cis-meQTLs passing FDR threshold.

claim: FOXO1, TERT and WNT4 showed significant meQTL associations.
source: Of the plausible predisposition genes, FOXO1, TERT and WNT4 showed significant meQTL associations (Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which predisposition genes showed significant meQTL associations.

claim: Telomere length was significantly shorter in tumors than in adjacent matched myometrium (p=0.01).
source: Overall the telomere length was significantly shorter in tumors than in adjacent matched myometrium (p=0.01; Kruskal-Wallis), as previously reported (Rogalla et al., 1995; Bonatz et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical comparison of telomere length between tumors and myometrium, and cites previous studies.

claim: One of the risk alleles at TERT (rs2736100) was significantly associated with shorter telomere length (p=0.01).
source: One of the risk alleles at TERT (rs2736100) was significantly associated with shorter telomere length (p=0.01; Kruskal-Wallis) (Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical association between this risk allele and telomere length.

claim: The association between rs2736100 and telomere length was not seen in myometrium.
source: The association was not seen in myometrium.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the association was specific to tumors.

claim: The other two LD-independent SNPs at TERT (rs72709458 and rs2853676) did not show association to telomere length.
source: The other two LD-independent SNPs at TERT, rs72709458 and rs2853676, or the SNPs at TERC (rs10936600) and OBFC1 (rs1265164) did not show association to telomere length (p=0.24, p=0.57, p=0.07 and p=0.48, respectively; Kruskal-Wallis).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the lack of association for these SNPs with telomere length.

claim: The SNPs at TERC (rs10936600) and OBFC1 (rs1265164) did not show association to telomere length.
source: The other two LD-independent SNPs at TERT, rs72709458 and rs2853676, or the SNPs at TERC (rs10936600) and OBFC1 (rs1265164) did not show association to telomere length (p=0.24, p=0.57, p=0.07 and p=0.48, respectively; Kruskal-Wallis).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the lack of association for these SNPs with telomere length.

claim: The combined effect of TERT, TERC and OBFC1 SNPs had a negative trend with telomere length (p=0.055).
source: The combined effect of TERT (rs72709458, rs2736100, rs2853676), TERC (rs10936600) and OBFC1 (rs1265164) had a negative trend with telomere length (p=0.055; linear model 95% CI −408.5 – 4.7 per one risk allele; see Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the combined effect of these SNPs on telomere length.

claim: No association was detected between genotype and the number of somatic structural variants in whole genome sequencing data.
source: In whole genome sequencing data, no association was detected between genotype and the number of somatic structural variants.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of association between genotype and structural variants.

claim: The DEPICT analysis did not reveal any significant pathway enrichments with the exception of one pathway related to induced stress.
source: The analysis did not reveal any significant enrichments with the exception of one pathway related to induced stress.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the results of the DEPICT pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: ATM was the highest ranking target gene in the DEPICT analysis.
source: ATM was the highest ranking target gene, and uterus/myometrium were among the highest ranking tissue types.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the top ranking gene from the DEPICT analysis.

claim: Uterus/myometrium were among the highest ranking tissue types in the DEPICT analysis.
source: ATM was the highest ranking target gene, and uterus/myometrium were among the highest ranking tissue types.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the top ranking tissue types from the DEPICT analysis.

claim: Two out of seven previously reported UL susceptibility loci replicated in UKBB: 22q13.1 (at TNRC6B) and 11p15.5 (at BET1L).
source: Two out of the seven loci - that is, 22q13.1 (at TNRC6B) and 11p15.5 (at BET1L) - replicated in UKBB using 15,453 cases and 392,628 controls.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which previously reported loci replicated in the current study.

claim: The OBFC1 region was identified in the discovery stage, though the specific SNP reported by Cha et al. did not replicate.
source: Cha et al (Cha et al., 2011). highlight OBFC1 (at 10q24.33) as a candidate gene and, while the SNP that they reported does not replicate in UKBB, the OBFC1 region is identified in our discovery stage (rs1265164; Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the OBFC1 region was identified, though the specific SNP from the previous study did not replicate.

claim: The top association at 6q25.2 (rs58415480) resides within intron 107 of SYNE1, 130 kb downstream of ESR1.
source: The top association at 6q25.2 (rs58415480) resides within intron 107 of Spectrin Repeat Containing Nuclear Envelope Protein 1 (SYNE1), 130 kb downstream of ESR1, the latter being the only gene that resides completely within the topologically associating domain (TAD; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the genomic location of the top association at this locus.

claim: ESR1 is the only gene that resides completely within the topologically associating domain at the 6q25.2 locus.
source: The top association at 6q25.2 (rs58415480) resides within intron 107 of Spectrin Repeat Containing Nuclear Envelope Protein 1 (SYNE1), 130 kb downstream of ESR1, the latter being the only gene that resides completely within the topologically associating domain (TAD; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that ESR1 is the only gene completely within the TAD at this locus.

claim: This is the first genetic evidence linking estrogen receptor to leiomyomagenesis.
source: While the role of estrogen in leiomyomagenesis has been firmly established, this is the first genetic evidence to this end.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that this is the first genetic evidence linking ESR1 to UL.

claim: The lead SNP at 2p resides in the third exon of the gene GREB1.
source: The lead SNP at 2 p resides in the third exon of the gene GREB1.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the genomic location of the lead SNP at this locus.

claim: GREB1 is an essential regulatory factor of ESR1.
source: GREB1 is an essential regulatory factor of ESR1 (Mohammed et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of GREB1 in ESR1 regulation.

claim: WT1, WNT4 and FOXO1 are central factors in uterine development and decidualization in endometrium.
source: WT1, WNT4 and FOXO1 are central factors in uterine development and in the preparation for pregnancy (decidualization) in endometrium (Biason-Lauber and Konrad, 2008; Hill, 2018; Kaya Okur et al., 2016; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support the role of these genes in uterine development.

claim: Perturbations in WT1, WNT4, and FOXO1 function are known to have neoplastic potential.
source: Perturbations in their function are known to have neoplastic potential.
evidence: The manuscript states that perturbations in these genes have neoplastic potential, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The strongest association at 11p13 (rs10835889) is 40 kb downstream of WT1, at a region with enhancer activity.
source: The strongest association at 11p13 (rs10835889) is 40 kb downstream of the closest gene WT1, at a region with enhancer activity (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the genomic location and regulatory context of this association.

claim: WT1 is a transcription factor that acts as both a tumor suppressor and an oncogene.
source: WT1 is a transcription factor that acts as both a tumor suppressor and an oncogene (Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the dual role of WT1.

claim: The lead SNP at 1p36.12 (rs2235529) resides at the second intron of WNT4.
source: The lead SNP at 1p36.12 (rs2235529) resides at the second intron of WNT4.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the genomic location of this SNP.

claim: The risk allele at 1p36.12 is associated with suggestive upregulation of WNT4.
source: The risk allele is associated with suggestive upregulation of WNT4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this association and references a figure showing the data.

claim: WNT4 is known to be overexpressed in uterine leiomyomas with MED12 mutations.
source: WNT4 is known to be overexpressed in uterine leiomyomas with MED12 mutations (Markowski et al., 2012), and knock-down of MED12 in UL cells reduces WNT4 expression (Al-Hendy et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support the overexpression of WNT4 in MED12-mutant ULs.

claim: Knock-down of MED12 in UL cells reduces WNT4 expression.
source: WNT4 is known to be overexpressed in uterine leiomyomas with MED12 mutations (Markowski et al., 2012), and knock-down of MED12 in UL cells reduces WNT4 expression (Al-Hendy et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the effect of MED12 knock-down on WNT4 expression.

claim: The risk locus in 1p36.12 was associated with several meQTLs suggesting that methylation may have a role in WNT4 regulation.
source: The risk locus in 1p36.12 was also associated with several meQTLs suggesting that methylation may have a role in WNT4 regulation (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this association and references a figure showing the meQTL data.

claim: WNT4 encodes a signaling protein that has a crucial role in sex-determination.
source: WNT4 encodes a signaling protein that has a crucial role in sex-determination (Vainio et al., 1999), and the WNT signaling pathway has a well-established role in various malignancies such as breast and ovarian cancer (Peltoketo et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support the role of WNT4 in sex determination.

claim: The WNT signaling pathway has a well-established role in various malignancies such as breast and ovarian cancer.
source: WNT4 encodes a signaling protein that has a crucial role in sex-determination (Vainio et al., 1999), and the WNT signaling pathway has a well-established role in various malignancies such as breast and ovarian cancer (Peltoketo et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of WNT signaling in cancer.

claim: A recent GWAS on gestational duration suggested that binding of the estrogen receptor at WNT4 is altered by rs3820282.
source: Of note, recent GWAS on gestational duration suggested that binding of the estrogen receptor at WNT4 is altered by rs3820282 (r2 = 0.92 with our lead SNP) (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published GWAS to support this observation about estrogen receptor binding.

claim: Both WNT4 and FOXO1 are decidualization markers regulated by ESR1.
source: Both WNT4 and FOXO1 are decidualization markers regulated by ESR1 (Kaya Okur et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the regulation of WNT4 and FOXO1 by ESR1.

claim: CDC42 has been shown to play a role in uterine pathology, in particular endometriosis.
source: Though these considerations support WNT4 as a candidate predisposition gene at this locus, the near-by CDC42 has been shown to play a role in uterine pathology, in particular endometriosis (Powell et al., 2016), and should not be overlooked in further work.
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of CDC42 in uterine pathology.

claim: MED12 has been implicated in uterine development in a mouse model.
source: Also MED12 has been implicated in uterine development in a mouse model (Wang et al., 2017a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of MED12 in uterine development.

claim: DMRT1 is a transcription factor associated with male sex-development.
source: DMRT1 is a transcription factor associated with male sex-development (Lindeman et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of DMRT1 in sex development.

claim: CD44 is a plausible fibroid stem cell marker.
source: CD44 is a plausible fibroid stem cell marker (Mas et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support CD44 as a fibroid stem cell marker.

claim: Mutations in SALL1 and a deletion at the GWAS signal have been associated with Townes-Brocks syndrome, a condition associated with kidney malformations.
source: Mutations in SALL1 and a deletion at the GWAS signal have been associated with Townes-Brocks syndrome, a condition associated with kidney malformations (Stevens and May, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the association of SALL1 with Townes-Brocks syndrome.

claim: The lead SNP at 11q (rs141379009) resides in the 22nd intron of ATM.
source: The lead SNP at 11q (rs141379009) resides in the 22nd intron of ATM, and the SNP at 17 p in the 3′-untranslated region of TP53.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the genomic location of this SNP.

claim: The lead SNP at 17p resides in the 3′-untranslated region of TP53.
source: The lead SNP at 11q (rs141379009) resides in the 22nd intron of ATM, and the SNP at 17 p in the 3′-untranslated region of TP53.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the genomic location of this SNP.

claim: ATM and TP53 are involved in DNA damage response.
source: ATM and TP53 are involved in DNA damage response (Guleria and Chandna, 2016), and they are among the relatively few genes that have been found to be recurrently mutated in leiomyosarcoma (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support the role of ATM and TP53 in DNA damage response.

claim: ATM and TP53 are among the relatively few genes that have been found to be recurrently mutated in leiomyosarcoma.
source: ATM and TP53 are involved in DNA damage response (Guleria and Chandna, 2016), and they are among the relatively few genes that have been found to be recurrently mutated in leiomyosarcoma (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the recurrent mutation of ATM and TP53 in leiomyosarcoma.

claim: TERT and TERC encode subunits of the telomerase enzyme, which guards chromosomal stability by elongating telomeres.
source: TERT and TERC encode subunits of the telomerase enzyme, which guards chromosomal stability by elongating telomeres (Blasco, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of TERT and TERC in telomere maintenance.

claim: OBFC1 has been associated with telomere maintenance.
source: In addition OBFC1 has been associated with telomere maintenance (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the role of OBFC1 in telomere maintenance.

claim: TERT is expressed in germ cells as well as in many types of cancers.
source: TERT is expressed in germ cells as well as in many types of cancers (Blasco, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support the expression pattern of TERT.

claim: The neoplasia predisposing effect of the risk alleles at the TERT locus has been overwhelmingly documented.
source: The neoplasia predisposing effect of the risk alleles at the TERT locus (rs72709458; rs2736100; rs2853676) has been overwhelmingly documented (Appendix 1—table 11).
evidence: The manuscript states that the neoplasia predisposing effect of TERT risk alleles is well-documented and references a table.

claim: Previous studies have reported contradicting observations on the effect of rs2736100 on telomere length.
source: Previous studies have reported contradicting observations on the effect of rs2736100 on telomere length (Liu et al., 2014; ENGAGE Consortium Telomere Group et al., 2014; Lan et al., 2013; Melin et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple published studies showing contradictory results on the effect of rs2736100 on telomere length.

claim: ULs have been shown to display shortened telomeres.
source: ULs have been shown to display shortened telomeres (Rogalla et al., 1995; Bonatz et al., 1998), potentially provoking chromosomal instability as the lengths of chromosome telomeres are diminished.
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies to support the observation of shortened telomeres in ULs.

claim: Shortened telomeres in ULs potentially provoke chromosomal instability.
source: ULs have been shown to display shortened telomeres (Rogalla et al., 1995; Bonatz et al., 1998), potentially provoking chromosomal instability as the lengths of chromosome telomeres are diminished.
evidence: The manuscript infers that shortened telomeres may lead to chromosomal instability based on established knowledge.

claim: GRS associated merely with a susceptibility to the most common UL subtype, MED12 mutation positive tumors.
source: GRS associated merely with a susceptibility to the most common UL subtype, MED12 mutation positive tumors.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that GRS was specifically associated with MED12 mutation positive tumors.

claim: It has been known that MED12-mutation-positive tumors do not distribute randomly among patients.
source: Indeed it has been known that MED12-mutation-positive tumors do not distribute randomly among patients (Mäkinen et al., 2011), and our data provide at least a partial explanation to this intriguing finding.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing non-random distribution of MED12-mutation-positive tumors.

claim: The risk allele near MED12 could facilitate selection of somatic MED12 mutations.
source: An outstanding susceptibility locus was identified 250 kb upstream of MED12: our in-house patient cohort - together with a mutation-screening of their 1481 tumors - revealed that the risk allele could facilitate selection of somatic MED12 mutations.
evidence: The manuscript infers that the risk allele may facilitate selection of somatic MED12 mutations based on the observed association.

claim: Environmental factors may contribute more significantly to genesis of MED12 wild-type lesions.
source: It may be that environmental factors contribute more significantly to genesis of MED12 wild-type lesions.
evidence: The manuscript speculates that environmental factors may be more important for MED12 wild-type lesions.

claim: A history of pelvic inflammatory disease was associated with MED12 wild-type tumor type in a recent study.
source: In our recent study this tumor type was associated with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease, and thus infectious agents could be one underlying factor (Heinonen et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study showing association between pelvic inflammatory disease and MED12 wild-type tumors.

claim: The power of GWAS to detect genetic associations to rare UL subtypes is reduced.
source: Obviously, also the power of GWAS to detect genetic associations to rare UL subtypes – such as the HMGA2 overexpressing or FH deficient subtypes – is reduced.
evidence: The manuscript infers that GWAS power is reduced for rare subtypes based on statistical principles.

claim: The proposed risk score can stratify the female population to low and high-risk quartiles that differ by two-fold in their UL risk.
source: The proposed risk score can stratify the female population to low and high-risk quartiles that differ by two-fold in their UL risk.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the stratification capability of the risk score.

claim: The population-specific risk score was inflated towards the African and Caribbean cohorts.
source: The population-specific risk score was inflated towards the African and Caribbean cohorts, which connects the predisposition loci to the excess UL prevalence in these ethnicities.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the risk score was higher in African and Caribbean populations.

claim: The inflated risk score in African and Caribbean populations connects the predisposition loci to the excess UL prevalence in these ethnicities.
source: The population-specific risk score was inflated towards the African and Caribbean cohorts, which connects the predisposition loci to the excess UL prevalence in these ethnicities.
evidence: The manuscript infers that the higher risk score explains part of the increased prevalence in these populations.

claim: The population-level burden to women's health arising from these risk loci is highly significant considering the incidence of the condition.
source: While the increased risk appears minor on an individual level, the population-level burden to women's health arising from these risk loci is highly significant considering the incidence of the condition.
evidence: The manuscript infers the population-level significance based on the high incidence of UL.

claim: The risk SNP at estrogen receptor alpha has the most immediate potential value.
source: The risk SNP with the most immediate potential value is that at estrogen receptor alpha, and our findings should fuel much further work on the interplay between individual germline genetics, endogenous and exogenous hormonal exposure, and occurrence and growth rate of UL.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the potential value of the ESR1 risk SNP.

claim: Figure 2C shows that the risk allele near MED12 (rs5937008) is observed with a significant increase in number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors (p=0.009; RR = 1.23 per risk allele; n = 457 Helsinki cohort patients).
source: (C), The risk allele near MED12 (rs5937008) is observed with a significant increase in number of MED12-mutation-positive tumors (p=0.009; negative binomial regression; RR = 1.23 per risk allele; n = 457 Helsinki cohort patients).
evidence: The figure caption explicitly describes the association shown in Figure 2C.
